question: A 169 kg cart is accelerated at a rate, in m/s², equal to 4 times the sum of 7 and 10. The cart is 1.8 m long. The depot runs 5 carts per line; each line's force is expressed in kilonewtons, and there are 10 lines. What is the total force, in kN?

A diagnostic reading q(t) = 2t³ + 5t² is logged over time t (seconds) on a test bench. Engineers take its rate of change, then take the rate of change of that result, and evaluate it at t = 4 seconds; this becomes the speed, in meters per second, of a 5 kg component. Find its kinetic energy, then multiply it by 2, by 8, and by 4 in turn, representing three successive production-batch multipliers. What is the final energy, in joules?

A laboratory report ends with one number in kilojoules. A trolley of mass 39 kg moves along a bench at a speed, in metres per second, equal to the exact area under the curve y = 1x^2 + 3x between x = 0 and x = 1. The energy the trolley carries because of that motion is the starting quantity. The technician adds 29 J to it for the energy already stored in the launch spring. That sum is then multiplied by 12, because 12 identical trolleys sit on the bench. The final line converts the result to kilojoules. A 7 L bottle of solvent stands on the same bench and plays no part. What is the number at the end of the report, in kJ?

A wind-tunnel log closes with one number in kilonewtons. The model cart on the balance has a mass plate reading 55000 g. Its commanded acceleration, in metres per second squared, is 5 multiplied by the sum of 6 and 5. The traverse motor must supply the force that gives the cart that acceleration, and the log writes that force in kilonewtons. With 7 carts on the traverse, the log multiplies that entry by 7, then subtracts 9 in the same kilonewton units for the balance tare. What is the closing number, in kN?

A test mass on a lab bench weighs 16,000 grams, that is, 16 kilograms. Two positive numbers add up to 9 and multiply together to 8; take the smaller of the two as the mass's speed, in meters per second, at release. Using that speed and the mass, its kinetic energy is found. The result, in joules, is converted into kilojoules, a recorded loss of 26 is then subtracted, a gain of 11 is added, and a further gain of 7 is added. The lab bench measures 2 meters across. What is the final energy, in kilojoules?

A quadratic solver finds the smaller root of x² - 10x + 21 = 0 (which is 3 m/s). A 18 kg mass yields energy, scaled by 2, converted to kilojoules, reduced by 10 kJ, and reduced by 8 kJ. What is the final energy in kilojoules?

A press line report closes with one number in newtons. A ram whose mass plate reads 106000 g is driven along its stroke. Its acceleration, in metres per second squared, is the slope of the curve y = 4x^3 + 3x^2 at x = 2. The drive must supply the force that gives that ram that acceleration. Eight rams work a press, so the press force is 8 times one ram's figure, from which 21 N is subtracted for guide friction and a further 26 N for the return spring. The plant runs 12 identical presses. What number closes the report, in N?

A rolling-mill sheet ends with one number in kilonewtons. A slab whose mass plate reads 136000 g is accelerated on the run-out table. Its acceleration, in metres per second squared, is 4 multiplied by the sum of 9 and 7. The rollers must supply the force that gives the slab that acceleration. Three tables work in parallel, so the mill force is 3 times one table's figure, and 30 N of drive preload is added to it. The sheet writes that in kilonewtons and then adds 23 in those same kilonewton units for the stand tare. A 250 L coolant sump serves the mill and is not involved. What number ends the sheet, in kN?

A quadratic solver finds the smaller root of x² - 12x + 35 = 0 (which is 5 m/s). A 36 kg mass at this speed yields energy, increased by 4 J, scaled by 5, converted to kilojoules, and scaled by 8. What is the final energy in kilojoules?

A lab's final energy reading, in kilojoules after a final subtraction of 1 kJ, is wanted — but it starts with two speed candidates. Two speeds, in m/s, sum to 3 and multiply to 2; the larger is kept, then doubled. This total speed belongs to a 59 kg slider. A separate thermometer reads 26°C, unrelated to this task. The slider's kinetic energy is converted into kilojoules, and finally 1 kJ is subtracted. What is the final energy, in kilojoules?

A rider and bike with a combined mass of 60,000 g move at a speed in m/s equal to 8 times the greatest common divisor of 279 and 80. Two riders form a pair, so the pair's combined energy of motion is twice that of one rider. Nine pairs race, so the race total is 9 times the pair value. From the race total, 1 J of timing loss is subtracted. What is the resulting figure, in J?

The final step of this lab's calculation always subtracts 4 from the joule reading right before it's recorded — keep that in mind. A test mass on a lab bench weighs 45 kilograms. A technician has 14 identical clips and 211 identical brackets and wants to divide them into the largest possible number of identical hardware sets with nothing left over; that largest number of sets, plus 2, gives the mass's speed, in meters per second, at release. Using that speed and the mass, its kinetic energy is found. The energy is then multiplied by 12 because twelve identical masses are released together, and a recorded gain of 3 is added. Finally, exactly as noted at the start, 4 is subtracted. What is the final energy, in joules?

A lab wants a final figure, in kilonewtons: 11 kN from a clamp, plus 6 kN from a spring, plus the force to accelerate a 5 kg cart, expressed in kilonewtons. The cart's acceleration, in m/s², equals the area under the curve y = 1·x² + 1·x from x = 1 to x = 2. The cart runs on an air track. What is the final figure, in kN?

A cyclist and bike with a combined mass of 48 kg ride on a velodrome at a speed in m/s equal to the larger root of x² - 7x + 10 = 0. A team of 8 such riders has a combined energy of motion 8 times that of one rider, and the coach converts that combined value to kJ. Three teams compete, so the meet figure is 3 times the team figure. Finally 23 kJ of stored reserve is added. What is the final figure, in kJ?

At a conveyor-belt test bench, a technician repeats a load test 5 times. Each repetition combines a baseline load worth 7 units with an extra load worth 6 units, and adding together the results from all 5 repetitions gives the total acceleration, in meters per second squared, of a gearbox housing with a mass of 80 kilograms. (The conveyor belt itself is 25 meters long, a fact that plays no role here.) Find the push this housing requires, in newtons, then convert that number into kilonewtons. Add 2 to the result, then subtract 28, and then subtract 20 more. What is the final number, in kilonewtons?

A demonstration bench launches a puck of 3 kg across a smooth surface. The puck's launch speed in metres per second is the smaller of the two values of x for which x^2 - 11x + 24 = 0. The bench records the energy the puck carries because of its motion and multiplies it by 7, because 7 launches make a demonstration. A fixed instrument offset of 8 J is added, the result is multiplied by 6 for the 6 demonstrations in the term, and a standing allowance of 4 J is added at the end. The bench is 1.2 m tall, a dimension that plays no part. What figure, in joules, does the bench report?
Solve x² - 15x + 56 = 0, smaller root. Subtract 25. Add 22. A mechanism with mass 120 kilograms has this acceleration. Calculate force. Scale by 6. What is the final force in Newtons?

Integrate ∫₀² (x² + 6x)dx = 14.667. With 18 kg, energy = 0.5 × 18 × (14.667)² ≈ 1936 J, convert to 1.936 kJ, plus 15 → 16.936, minus 10 → 6.936, times 7. The loop count is 1000. What is the final energy in kJ?

Calculate 6 choose 3, yielding 20. A generator with mass 18 kilograms uses this velocity. Calculate kinetic energy. Scale by 11. Convert to kiloJoules. Add 16. Scale by 10. What is the final energy in kiloJoules?

A counting sequence sums from 1 to 12, yielding 78. This total becomes the acceleration in m/s² for an 8 kg test element. The resulting force converts to kilonewtons. Adding 7 kN from support increases it. This adjusted value is amplified by 9 times for the load distribution. What is the final distributed load in kN? (The element's width is 30 cm, which is not relevant.)

A gear-cutting shop needs the net figure, in kilojoules, at the foot of its test sheet. Two index plates carry 154 holes and 380 holes, and the setter needs the largest whole number that divides both counts exactly. The test slider is then run at a speed, in metres per second, numerically equal to that number, and the slider has a mass of 35 kg. To the energy the slider carries by virtue of that motion the sheet adds 29 J for the latch, then subtracts 29 J for the release, and expresses the result in kilojoules. A standing instrument allowance of 30 kJ is finally subtracted. What is the net figure, in kJ?
Solve x² - 5x + 4 = 0, larger root. Scale by 5. A spring with mass 8 kilograms has this velocity. Calculate kinetic energy. Scale by 7. Scale by 11. What is the final energy in Joules?

An energy system selects velocity from polynomial x² - 5x + 4, choosing the larger root (4 m/s), scaled 9 times to 36 m/s, then scaled 2 more times to 72 m/s for a 16 kg mass. Kinetic energy is calculated, reduced by 21 J for losses, then converted to kJ. What is the final stored energy in kJ?

On a lab test cart, acceleration follows a(t) = 2t² + 2t (in m/s², t in seconds); the speed gained between t = 2 s and t = 3 s belongs to a cart whose mass is stated as 40000 grams. A separate voltmeter reads 5 V, unrelated to this task. From the resulting kinetic energy, 2 J is added, the total is scaled by a factor of 7, and finally converted into kilojoules. What is the final energy, in kilojoules?

A 31 kg service robot is driven across a factory floor. Its acceleration, in m/s², is 5 times the area under the curve y = 3x² + 4x from x = 0 to x = 1. The robot's drive controller reports the force needed for this acceleration in kilonewtons and then adds a fixed 10 kN reserve for its tow hitch. The factory runs 12 identical robots from one power bus, each with the same reserve. What total force, in kN, does the power bus have to be rated for?
